plan.contextChunk: This figure plots Archimedes' spiral on a single polar grid across one full turn. The grid is a set of concentric gray circles about the origin crossed by gray radial spokes, with horizontal and vertical axes numbered by integers from -7 to 7 in both directions and tipped with arrowheads. A solid dark navy curve starts at the origin and sweeps counterclockwise, its distance from the center growing steadily as it goes, so the trace forms one open loop that never crosses itself and finishes on the positive horizontal axis at about six units out. Six filled black dots mark sample points along the curve, each tagged with an ordered pair whose two entries are equal: (pi/4, pi/4) just above and right of the origin, (pi/2, pi/2) directly above it near height 1.6, (pi, pi) out to the left at about three units, (5pi/4, 5pi/4) down and to the left, (7pi/4, 7pi/4) down and to the right, and (2pi, 2pi) at the loop's end on the right. Because the radius listed in each pair matches the angle listed beside it, the marked dots let the reader confirm the relation r = theta point by point, and the even widening of the loop between successive crossings of a given direction is what a radius growing in direct proportion to the swept angle looks like.

interactionPlan.concept: Archimedes' spiral r = θ is produced when a point's distance from the origin grows in exact proportion to the angle it has swept, so steady angular motion yields a curve that widens by an equal amount on every turn.
elements: polar grid: concentric gray circles centered at the origin at integer radii 1 through 7
eight gray radial spokes at 45° increments crossing the circles
horizontal axis with arrowheads at both ends and integer tick labels -7 to 7
vertical axis with arrowheads at both ends and integer tick labels -7 to 7
solid dark-navy spiral curve starting at the origin and sweeping counterclockwise one full turn, ending near (6.28, 0) on the positive horizontal axis
six filled black sample dots on the curve at θ = π/4, π/2, π, 5π/4, 7π/4, 2π
label (π/4, π/4) near the first dot, upper-right of origin
label (π/2, π/2) above the origin near height 1.6
label (π, π) to the left near radius 3
label (5π/4, 5π/4) lower-left
label (7π/4, 7π/4) lower-right
label (2π, 2π) at the curve's right end near radius 6
dynamic moving point on the spiral driven by the θ slider
dynamic radius vector line from origin to the moving point
dynamic readout showing current θ value and matching r value
highlightable angle ray (spoke direction) and highlightable concentric radius circle for clicked sample points

interactions.label: Trace the spiral
interactions.teaches: The spiral is generated by two simultaneous motions: a radius vector rotating at constant angular speed while its length increases steadily, leaving the curve behind — angle and radius advance together from the very start

interactions.label: θ (radians)
interactions.teaches: Dragging θ moves the point along the spiral and the radius readout always equals the angle readout, confirming point by point that r = θ
Clicking a labeled dot highlights its angle ray and the concentric circle of the same value intersecting there, making visible why both entries of each polar coordinate (θ, θ) are equal

demo_steps.title: Watch the spiral form
demo_steps.narration: Play the trace: a radius vector rotates counterclockwise at constant speed while steadily lengthening, drawing the navy curve. The even widening between successive passes of any direction is the signature of radius growing in direct proportion to angle.

demo_steps.title: Radius equals angle
demo_steps.narration: Drag the θ slider and watch the readouts: at every position the radius value matches the angle value exactly. At θ = π the point sits precisely on the circle of radius π, out to the left.

demo_steps.title: Confirm at the sample points
demo_steps.narration: Sweep to θ = 2π at the loop's end, then click individual dots such as (π, π) or (7π/4, 7π/4): the highlighted ray and the highlighted concentric circle meet exactly at the dot, showing both polar coordinates are the same number.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because r = θ, a point moving at constant angular speed also moves outward at constant radial speed — that single proportionality is what makes Archimedes' spiral widen by an equal gap on every turn.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Center the polar grid in a square viewport; concentric circles and 45° spokes in light gray, axes in black with arrowheads and integer labels -7..7 on both axes. Draw the spiral as a smooth dark-navy stroke from the origin through one full counterclockwise turn ending near (6.28, 0). Place six solid black dots at the listed angles with their (θ, θ) labels in italic math styling positioned just outside the curve as in the source (π/4 upper-right, π/2 above, π left, 5π/4 lower-left, 7π/4 lower-right, 2π right). The moving point and its radius vector should be a contrasting accent color (e.g. red) with a small live readout panel showing θ and r to two decimals so their equality is obvious. On click, highlight the matching spoke ray and the matching concentric circle in the same accent color while dimming the rest of the grid slightly.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for theta: the learner drags theta from 0 to 2pi, the point travels along the spiral while the radius readout matches the angle readout, making the relation r = theta visible point by point.
- Animation for tracing the spiral: a rotating radius sweeps counterclockwise and leaves the curve behind as it lengthens, showing that Archimedes' spiral is produced by steady angular motion paired with steadily increasing distance from the origin.
- Click for sample points: the learner clicks a labeled dot such as (pi, pi) or (7pi/4, 7pi/4), its angle ray and matching radius circle highlight together, clarifying why both entries in each plotted polar coordinate are equal.

authoredContext:
Notice that the r-values are just the decimal form of the angle measured in radians. We can see them on a graph in the figure.

Archimedes’ spiral

Graph of Archimedes' spiral r=theta over [0,2pi]. Starts at origin and spirals out in one loop counterclockwise. Points (pi/4, pi/4), (pi/2,pi/2), (pi,pi), (5pi/4, 5pi/4), (7pi/4, pi/4), and (2pi, 2pi) are marked.

discrepancies: The default (step-0) view shows a conspicuous red tracer dot at the origin plus a red 'θ = 0.00 r = 0.00' readout line near the top of the y-axis, neither of which exists in the static source (the source has a plain black dot at the origin and no readout).
The spiral's start point at the origin is rendered red (the interactive tracer) in the generated default state, whereas the source shows it as a black sample dot.
Sample-point coordinate labels are drawn at ~11px, only marginally larger than the 10px axis tick numbers, so the source's clear hierarchy (large coordinate labels vs small ticks) is weakened.
evaluation.notes: The Archimedean spiral r = θ, polar grid, axes, tick range, navy curve, and all six (r, θ) sample points with correct coordinates are faithfully reproduced, and the slider/trace-animation/click-to-highlight interactions are pedagogically excellent; the main weaknesses are cosmetic — a red tracer dot and readout that intrude on the otherwise-static default view and slightly undersized coordinate labels.
action_items: At the default step-0 state, render the moving tracer dot in black (or hide it and the red readout until the slider/animation is first used) so the static default matches the source's black origin dot and has no extra red text.
Increase the sample-point coordinate label font size to ~13-14px so they clearly dominate the 10px tick numbers, restoring the source's label hierarchy.
Keep the red readout text but move it into the #ui panel (or fade it in only during interaction) so it does not sit on the plot area at the top of the y-axis in the resting state.

feedback.rationale: Overall average of 4.6 with no failure modes and only minor cosmetic discrepancies (tracer dot color, slightly undersized labels) indicates the figure is high quality and further iteration would yield negligible improvement.
